transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-22
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Camila (Redwood SE), Marcus (Redwood Product), Amina, Ben, Rafael, Sofia (Silvershore)

Optional auto-generated summary: (may be noisy) Redwood demo — structured output gates + tool calls, console sandbox, security Qs, pilot next steps.

[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, I'm the AE on this account. Quick intros?
[00:06] Amina Noor: Hi, I'm Amina, lead ML at Silvershore. We own the recommendation models and the assistant project.
[00:11] Ben Chu: Ben, platform eng, I'll be handling deployment and infra questions.
[00:14] Rafael Ortega: Rafael, security. I'll be validating compliance needs.
[00:16] Sofia Tran: Sofia, PM for the assistant.
[00:18] Camila Ruiz: Camila, solutions engineer at Redwood. I'll demo JSON mode and runtime gates.
[00:21] Marcus Lee: Marcus, product, I'll chime on Optimize recommendations.

[00:30] Jordan Patel: Great. Goal for today is to show how Redwood enforces structured outputs and how tool calling works with guardrails — we call this "gates" in the runtime — and then walk the console sandbox plus some Optimize recommendations. Also answer security and deployment Qs.

[00:45] Amina Noor: High level — we have an assistant that needs to call internal services for account lookup and policy checks. The business asks: can we guarantee the model returns a typed payload so our orchestration layer can safely call services? Also we have data residency and encryption needs.

[01:10] Camila Ruiz: Yes. So first piece — JSON mode with typed schemas. You author a JSON schema, upload to console or via API, and the runtime will try to enforce the shape. We then layer runtime gates: field-level validators, policy filters (e.g., blacklist PII fields from being emitted), and automatic fallback to a safe stub if the schema is violated.

[01:37] Ben Chu: When you say "enforce" how hard is enforce? I mean, we still parse natural language, won't it hallucinate keys or junk?

[01:47] Camila Ruiz: Great question. It's probabilistic enforcement. The runtime applies a multi-step strategy: prompt-level constraints + a deterministic post-parse validator. If validator fails, there's configurable behaviors — reject, sanitize, or fall back to another model variant. We also offer a pre-commit sandbox that shows divergence rates on your prompt set.

[02:10] Rafael Ortega: How's PII handled? We want to avoid any customer SSNs leaving our environment.

[02:17] Marcus Lee: On the security side we support private deployments (VPC or on-prem), customer KMS integration for key sealing, and audit logs. For hosted, we still have token isolation and SOC 2 controls. But if you need full separation, Redwood Private is available.

[02:42] Amina Noor: For latency-sensitive flows, we might prefer Dedicated. Does the schema enforcement add a lot of latency?

[02:50] Camila Ruiz: Minimal — most of the enforcement is after the token stream. We can stream tokens while running a light-weight validator in the runtime. Worst case, a failed validation triggers a quick re-run with a constrained model; that adds an additional round-trip but we expose metrics so you can set SLOs. Marcus can go into Optimize suggestions for batching/noise tradeoffs.

[03:15] Marcus Lee: Sure — for high QPS with low latency, dedicated pools + smaller quantized variants tend to win on cost. But JSON mode often benefits from slightly larger context models to reduce structural errors. Our Optimize tool will recommend a quantization profile (e.g., 4-bit LLMQ) and batching window based on your observed distribution.

[03:45] Sofia Tran: Can you demo a sample flow where the assistant returns a typed action and then calls an internal API?

[03:52] Camila Ruiz: Yep. Switching to the console — I'll share my screen. 
[04:05] [screen share noise / brief silence]
[04:10] Camila Ruiz: Ok, console view — on the left is models, center is playground. I'm loading a schema called "account_lookup_v1". It's simple: { account_id: string, require_2fa: boolean, confidence: number, actions: array }. I run a sample prompt: "Find account by email and return action payload".
[04:40] [00:04:41] Speaker 1: (mumble) the transcript engine sometimes merges tokens, sorry.
[04:48] Camila Ruiz: Output in JSON mode — see the typed object. Now I deliberately send a prompt with ambiguous email and the validator flags 'confidence' below threshold. The runtime's gate policy is set to 'require_confirmation' so it returns a structured response with an extra field 'requires_human' and then a safe tool call to a 'verify_email' microservice stub.
[05:25] Amina Noor: Wait, 'safe tool call' — what's the contract there?
[05:29] Camila Ruiz: Tools are defined with an OpenAPI-like surface. You register a tool in the Console, provide the schema of inputs, and the runtime will map model output fields to tool inputs. We also offer a policy layer that can block outbound calls if the payload contains red-flag fields. So the model cannot directly exfiltrate arbitrary text to a network endpoint.
[05:52] Ben Chu: So mapping is deterministic? And if the model mis-labels a field will it still call wrong API?
[05:58] Camila Ruiz: The mapping is guarded by the validator. If the validator fails to match types, call is blocked and marked in the audit log. You can configure auto-sanitization, or require manual review. The sandbox will show you false positive/negative rates for your prompts.
[06:20] Rafael Ortega: Audit logs — what do they contain?
[06:23] Marcus Lee: Full token-level trace (configurable retention), tool invocation records, which model variant served, runtime policy decisions, and KMS key IDs used. We can redact tokens in hosted logs if you require.
[06:37] [00:06:40] Speaker 2: there's sometimes cross talk, sorry about speaker IDs.
[06:45] Amina Noor: Could you show a failure path where the model outputs malformed JSON and how Redwood recovers?
[06:52] Camila Ruiz: Yes. I'll run an aggressive prompt. [runs prompt] The model emits extra comments and a stray comma. The post-parse validator fails. Because the policy is set to 'fallback-model', Redwood re-invokes a smaller deterministic model with a strict system instruction "only output JSON matching schema" and returns a corrected payload. The original failed output is stored in the logs for analysis and retrain signal.
[07:25] Ben Chu: Interesting — does that cost double tokens?
[07:28] Camila Ruiz: Only in the failure path — the second call consumes additional tokens. Optimize flags these failure rates so you can choose stricter prompt engineering or a different model.
[07:38] Sofia Tran: On the topic of retries, can we set a budget of max retries and a latency cap?
[07:44] Marcus Lee: Yes, rollout policies include max_retries, total_latency_ms, and fallback behaviors: return stub, escalate to human, or route to a cheaper model. Those are configurable per route.
[07:55] Amina Noor: For the tool calling pattern — does Redwood execute tools within the same VPC if we use Private?
[08:00] Camila Ruiz: If you deploy Redwood Private in your VPC or on-prem, tool endpoints remain within your network. For hosted, we support outbound VPC peering and tunnel options. In all setups you can enforce egress rules so tool calls never leave your network.
[08:18] Rafael Ortega: KMS integration — we need CMEK for stored artifacts.
[08:22] Marcus Lee: We support customer-managed keys for Private deployments and bring-your-own-key for certain hosted tiers. We'll include cryptographic attestation in the security pack.
[08:34] [00:08:35] Speaker 3: (laugh) the auto caption spelled 'KMS' as 'K M S' earlier, transcript quirk.
[08:41] Camila Ruiz: Back to demo — now I'll show runtime gates UI. On the console you can add a gate: schema enforcement, PII redaction, URL sanitizer, and routing rule. I'm adding a gate that blocks any outgoing tool call if 'confidence' < 0.65 and tags it for human review.
[09:05] Amina Noor: Can gates call external policy engines? We already have an internal policy decision point (PDP).
[09:12] Camila Ruiz: Yes — gates can call your PDP synchronously via a policy webhook. You define the decision contract, and Redwood will evaluate it before executing a tool. We also cache decisions to reduce latency for repeated calls.
[09:30] Ben Chu: Caching decisions — what's the TTL and how do you invalidate?
[09:35] Camila Ruiz: TTLs configurable; we support explicit invalidation via API calls and event hooks when your internal state changes.
[09:42] Sofia Tran: How do you handle streaming outputs and validator checks mid-stream? Does the UI show partials?
[09:48] Camila Ruiz: Yes, streaming works. Validator runs on prefixes and can signal early if a required field appears unlikely. The console shows a live stream with inline validation markers. If a field looks wrong, the runtime can preemptively request more context or escalate.
[10:10] Amina Noor: For our on-call flow we need end-to-end traceability and ability to replay an invocation for debugging.
[10:17] Marcus Lee: We store invocation traces and you can replay them in the sandbox with the same model variant, seed, and policy settings. Traces are tied to audit IDs.
[10:27] Rafael Ortega: Retention windows? We need 90-day access minimum for logs.
[10:32] Marcus Lee: We support configurable retention — 30/90/365 days for logs; long-term archive options are available for enterprise.
[10:40] [00:10:41] Speaker 1: (brief overlap)
[10:45] Camila Ruiz: Now a quick look at function/tool chaining — I'm defining two tools: account_lookup and verify_2fa. The model returns actions: [ { name: "account_lookup", input: { email: "..." } } ]. The runtime maps that to an internal stub call and returns the tool response back to the model in the next turn if configured.
[11:12] Ben Chu: So you support multi-step tool chains where the model's output drives subsequent calls?
[11:16] Camila Ruiz: Exactly. You can configure synchronous chaining or queued async calls. For synchronous, we stream the tool response back in a bounded format; for async, the runtime emits an event and you can consume it.
[11:28] Amina Noor: Are there safeguards to prevent infinite loops where the model keeps calling tools?
[11:32] Camila Ruiz: Yes — max_chain_length, total_token_budget, and per-tool rate limits. These are enforced at runtime.
[11:38] Sofia Tran: Does Optimize recommend chain settings?
[11:40] Marcus Lee: Optimize runs simulations on your prompt set and suggests chain_length caps, batching windows, and whether to enable KV cache for repeated context. For account lookup, KV cache reduces lookups massively when the same account appears frequently.
[11:56] Ben Chu: On KV cache — is that safe for PII?
[11:59] Marcus Lee: KV cache can be configured with encryption at rest and selective TTL, and you can choose not to cache PII fields. It's per-route configurable.
[12:12] Rafael Ortega: Regarding compliance, can we run the platform in an air-gapped environment?
[12:17] Marcus Lee: For Private deployments we offer an air-gapped on-prem bundle. It requires an enterprise contract and our deployment team will run the install with your SREs.
[12:28] Amina Noor: Ok, two more things: cost estimate for pilot and a short perf window to run sample prompts.
[12:35] Jordan Patel: We'll produce a pilot scope with pricing tiers: hosted pilot, dedicated small pool, or private. Camila and Marcus, can you provide perf back-of-envelope and a recommended config for 500 qps bursts?
[12:47] Camila Ruiz: For 500 QPS bursts you'd want dedicated pools with autoscale and burst capacity. Use batching for throughputy calls and single-token streaming for interactive actions. Quantization helps, but for structured output we suggest a medium-sized model (e.g., 7B-13B depending on noise tolerance) with 4-bit quantization as a starting point. We'll run a quick estimate after this call.
[13:10] Ben Chu: We will need region: we prefer eu-west-1 for data residency.
[13:14] Jordan Patel: Noted. We'll include eu-west-1 in pilot options.
[13:18] Rafael Ortega: Onboarding and SSO — we need SAML + SCIM for provisioning and RBAC for roles.
[13:24] Camila Ruiz: Supported — SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and granular RBAC at route/model level.
[13:30] [00:13:31] Speaker 2: (brief background noise)
[13:35] Amina Noor: Can you email a security pack with SOC2, pen test summary, and KMS design?
[13:40] Jordan Patel: Yes we'll send the security pack. That's one of the next steps.
[13:45] Camila Ruiz: Final demo snippet — I'm going to show a failure injection: the model calls account_lookup but returns an extra field 'export_url' which our gate strips and logs as a policy violation. The tool call is blocked and the system returns an action 'requires_human' to the orchestration layer.
[14:12] Sofia Tran: Nice — can you slide in how the console surfaces these violations?
[14:16] Camila Ruiz: The violation view shows the input, the emitted payload, which gate failed, and suggested remediation. You can also create a rule in-console to auto-sanitize certain fields.
[14:30] Amina Noor: Walk me through how we'd run a pilot — timeline and expected deliverables.
[14:35] Jordan Patel: Typical pilot: 2-4 week evaluation. Week 1: integration + sample dataset upload. Week 2: run prompts and tune gates. Week 3: perf window and cost tuning with Optimize and recommended quant profiles. Week 4: closing review and production checklist. We can compress timelines if Silvershore provides prompt sets and infra access quickly.
[14:58] Ben Chu: We can prepare sample prompt sets and a staging VPC by end of week.
[15:02] Rafael Ortega: Security review will need an initial review cycle — we'll aim for sign-off within three weeks if everything looks good.
[15:08] Jordan Patel: Great. Quick recap of agreed next steps: Jordan send pilot scope + pricing, Camila send console recording + quickstart, Marcus send initial perf recommendations, Amina provide prompts.
[15:22] Amina Noor: Sounds good. Any other product notes?
[15:25] Marcus Lee: One more — Optimize will provide cost-vs-latency curves per route. We'll include token cost estimates in the pilot sheet so you can decide whether to route low-risk traffic to cheaper models.
[15:37] Ben Chu: Any special network setup for hosted to do egress restrictions?
[15:41] Camila Ruiz: We recommend setting up a VPC peering with strict egress ACLs and use our tunnel option for initial work. For production, Private gives you full control.
[15:52] [00:15:53] Speaker 1: overlap, slight echo on caller 2.
[16:00] Jordan Patel: Ok wrapping up. We'll send the materials and propose a benchmark slot next Tuesday. Who should we list as the primary technical contact?
[16:09] Amina Noor: Ben and I will share contact details; Ben is primary infra.
[16:14] Rafael Ortega: And I'll be on the security thread.
[16:16] Jordan Patel: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the pilot doc and security pack.
[16:21] Camila Ruiz: Thanks — bye.
[16:22] Meeting end.
